title: They took two-thirds of one amino acid out of the chow, and the male mice lived 23% longer

study.citation: Calubag, M. F., Ademi, I., Green, C. L., Manchanayake, D. N. H., Jayarathne, H. S. M., Marshall, R. N., Le, S. M., Lialios, P., Breuer, L. E., Yakar, S., Babygirija, R., Sonsalla, M. M., Grunow, I., Yeh, C.-Y., Liu, Y., Knopf, B. A., Yandell, S., Opara, C. I., Ricke, W. A., Liu, T. T., Keller, M. P., Attie, A. D., Sadagurski, M. & Lamming, D. W. (2026), "Lifelong restriction of dietary valine has sex-specific benefits for health and lifespan in mice", Nature Aging

tldr: Cutting one of the twenty amino acids in protein by two-thirds made mice of both sexes leaner and less frail for life, and it stretched median male lifespan by 23%.

sections.body: Protein has a spotless reputation. It fills you up, it builds muscle, and older adults are routinely told to eat more of it. Aging research keeps complicating that story. Feeding animals less protein tends to make them healthier and longer-lived, and the effect seems to run through a small subgroup of protein's building blocks called the branched-chain amino acids: leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Restricting all three together has extended male mouse lifespan by more than 30 percent. Isoleucine alone works. Leucine alone does close to nothing. Valine had never been tested over a whole lifetime, so a Wisconsin lab ran the experiment.

They raised 148 mice, half male and half female, on custom chow starting at four weeks of age, which is barely past weaning, and kept them on it until they died. Half got a normal amount of valine. Half got 67 percent less. Everything else was held equal: same calories, same fat, same carbohydrate, and the missing valine was replaced with a bit more of the amino acids the body builds for itself, so the share of calories from protein never changed. Thirty-seven mice per group per sex. The team weighed them monthly, scanned body composition twice a year, ran glucose tests, timed them on a rotating rod, and scored a 28-item frailty checklist.

Male mice on the low-valine chow lived 23 percent longer at the median. Female mice got no lifespan gain at all. Both sexes, though, aged better: they put on weight more slowly, carried less fat, scored lower on the frailty checklist, and showed fewer inflammatory markers in the brain. Females did better on a memory test. Males handled a sugar load better starting at three months old and were still handling it better at two years. The strange part is the bookkeeping. The low-valine mice ate more calories for their body size and stayed leaner anyway, because they were burning more, and the extra burn came from heat production rather than from moving around more.

Longevity nutrition has spent decades arguing about amounts: how many calories, how many grams of protein, how many hours between meals. This result pushes the argument toward composition. One amino acid out of twenty, dialed down while everything else stays put, was enough to reshape a mouse's whole aging trajectory. The molecular trail is interesting too. The benefits tracked with a turned-down PI3K-Akt pathway, a growth-signaling relay whose quieting has extended life in worms, flies, and mice. That dial moved in males, which is the sex that gained years, and it gives researchers something specific to chase in a field full of vague talk about metabolism.

These are mice, one inbred strain, one level of restriction, started at four weeks old. Interventions that begin in near-infancy translate poorly to humans who would start in middle age, and the authors say so plainly. They also note that a different degree of restriction might have helped the females, since 67 percent was the only dose tried. Thirty-seven animals per group is respectable for a lifespan study and still small enough that the survival curves carry real uncertainty. No human has eaten this diet, and valine sits inside meat, dairy, eggs, and whey, so there is no clean way to cut it at the grocery store. The senior author discloses an advisory role at a company developing drugs in a related pathway.

terms.def: Leucine, isoleucine, and valine, three of the twenty building blocks that make up protein; your body cannot manufacture them, so all of yours came from food, and they are especially concentrated in meat, dairy, eggs, and whey powder.
A scored checklist of visible age-related problems, from a hunched spine to cloudy eyes to a poor coat, averaged into one number that says roughly how worn down an animal is.
A chemical relay inside cells that reacts to food and growth signals; turning it down has lengthened life in worms, flies, and mice, which is why aging researchers watch it closely.

takeaways: Removing two-thirds of a single amino acid, with calories and every other nutrient held constant, added 23 percent to median male mouse lifespan.
Living longer and aging better came apart here: females got the leanness, the lower frailty, and the better memory scores while gaining no extra time.
The low-valine mice ate more and stayed leaner because they burned more as heat, which is a reminder that 'calories in, calories out' has a moving right-hand side.

quiz.q: Why does it matter that the two diets had identical calories, fat, carbohydrate, and total protein share?
choices: It let the researchers feed the mice less overall
It isolates valine as the variable, so the results cannot be explained by eating less or by a general protein cut
It made the chow cheaper to produce
It guaranteed the mice would eat the same amount
quiz.why: Calorie restriction and general protein restriction already have known longevity effects. By matching everything except valine, and by refilling the gap with amino acids the body can make on its own, the team made sure any difference in outcome pointed at valine itself.

quiz.q: What happened to the female mice on the low-valine diet?
choices: They lived 23 percent longer, same as the males
They got worse on every measure
They gained healthspan benefits like lower body fat, lower frailty, and better memory scores, with no gain in lifespan
They were excluded from the lifespan analysis
quiz.why: This is the sex-specific part of the finding. Females showed the metabolic and frailty improvements and did better on a memory test, and their survival curve still landed on top of the control females. The authors suspect a different level of restriction might change that, which no one has tested yet.

quiz.q: The low-valine mice ate more calories relative to their body size and were still leaner. What explained it?
choices: They ran on the wheel far more than control mice
They absorbed less of their food and lost the rest
Their energy expenditure rose, driven by heat production rather than by extra movement
They were weighed at a different time of day
quiz.why: Metabolic chamber measurements showed higher energy expenditure in the restricted mice, and spontaneous activity was unchanged, which points at heat generation. That is why leanness showed up without any reduction in how much they ate.
